title: Give an overview of the industry structure

lessons.title: The structure of South African agriculture
lessons.html:
A dual agricultural sector

South African agriculture has a highly developed commercial sector alongside a large number of smallholder and subsistence farmers. Commercial farms produce most marketed output, while smallholders are important for household food security, rural livelihoods and growing commercial participation through land reform and development programmes.

Main sub-sectors

  • Field crops: maize (the staple and the largest field crop), wheat, sunflower, soybeans, sugarcane, sorghum.
  • Horticulture: citrus, deciduous fruit (apples, pears, table grapes, stone fruit), subtropical fruit (avocados, mangoes, macadamias), vegetables, potatoes, wine grapes and flowers. Horticulture is a major export earner.
  • Livestock: beef cattle, dairy, sheep and goats (meat, wool and mohair), poultry (broilers and eggs, the largest animal protein sector), pigs and game.
  • Forestry and others: plantations, rooibos, honeybush and aquaculture.

The value chain

Agriculture is part of a wider value chain:

  1. Input suppliers: seed, fertiliser, chemicals, feed, machinery, finance and insurance.
  2. Primary producers: farms of all sizes.
  3. Handling and storage: silos, packhouses, cold stores, feedlots.
  4. Processing: mills, abattoirs, dairies, wineries, juice and canning factories.
  5. Distribution and marketing: fresh produce markets, wholesalers, retailers, exporters, informal traders.
  6. Consumers: local and export.

Most of the value of food is added beyond the farm gate, which is why many farms try to move into processing, packing or direct marketing.

Regional diversity

Climate drives farming patterns: grain and cattle on the Highveld; fruit and wine in the Western Cape; sugarcane and forestry along the KwaZulu-Natal and Mpumalanga coasts and escarpment; citrus and subtropicals in Limpopo, Mpumalanga and the Eastern Cape; extensive sheep and game in the Karoo and drier west.

lessons.title: Organisations, government and the regulatory environment
lessons.html:
Government

The national department responsible for agriculture sets policy, administers key legislation, runs veterinary and plant health services, manages export certification arrangements and supports smallholder development. Provincial departments of agriculture deliver extension services, veterinary services and support programmes. Other departments deal with water, environment, labour and trade.

Statutory and parastatal bodies

  • Agricultural Research Council (ARC): national agricultural research.
  • National Agricultural Marketing Council (NAMC): advises on marketing policy and administers statutory levies under the Marketing of Agricultural Products Act 47 of 1996.
  • Perishable Products Export Control Board (PPECB): export quality inspections and cold chain services for perishable products.
  • Land Bank: development finance for agriculture.
  • AgriSETA: skills development and training quality assurance for the sector.

Organised agriculture and commodity organisations

Farmers organise through national and provincial farmers' unions and associations representing commercial, emerging and smallholder farmers. Commodity organisations represent specific industries, for example grain, citrus, fruit, red meat, poultry, milk, wool and sugar. They provide market information, research, lobbying, training and often manage statutory levy funds.

Private sector players

Agribusinesses, many of them former co-operatives, supply inputs, finance, storage and marketing. Retailers, processors and exporters strongly influence standards through supplier requirements.

Regulatory environment

  • Agricultural remedies, fertilisers, feeds and stock remedies: Act 36 of 1947
  • Animal diseases: Animal Diseases Act 35 of 1984
  • Meat safety: Meat Safety Act 40 of 2000
  • Resource conservation: Act 43 of 1983
  • Water use: National Water Act 36 of 1998
  • Labour and safety: BCEA, LRA, OHS Act 85 of 1993
  • Export standards: Agricultural Product Standards Act 119 of 1990

Trade

South Africa is a net exporter of agricultural products. Exports depend on trade agreements, phytosanitary and veterinary access, and exchange rates.

Key points

  • The sector combines commercial and smallholder farming.
  • Main sub-sectors are field crops, horticulture, livestock and forestry.
  • Agriculture sits in a value chain from inputs to consumers.
  • Government, statutory bodies, organised agriculture and agribusiness shape the industry.
  • Legislation governs inputs, animal health, resources, labour and exports.
